title: HTTP: Incorrect request/response matching
description:
If the I/O is asynchronous (yet ordered) requests and responses were being matched via LIFO rather than FIFO. 
The display of the next and previous request and response has been eliminated because there is no use case for them and it bloated the Packet Display.

When the capture is closed, req_list links will be freed and req-list will be NULL. I've tested with this change and all is well. I think I'll submit this as a unique MR.

This change removed the `http.response_for.uri` field originally introduced by this feature request https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/issues/15344.

Was it intended to be deprecated and replaced by something better / is there a technical reason the field can't be reliably computed?

That filter was replaced with "http.request.full_uri" which returns requests and responses for a given URI or all the frames containing
that field name. If you only want responses, you can use "http.request.full_uri and tcp.srcport == 9000" or whatever
the source port of the server was. Does this satisfy your needs?

I agree that in principle, it should be possible to do the same tracking.

It's a bit inconvenient that the change isn't backwards compatible - I wasn't expecting to have to make changes to my Lua dissector on a minor version bump - but I should be able to adapt it.

It'll have to be more stateful to properly track whether it's a request or response compared to just checking for `http.response_for.uri`, but that's par for the course for any kind of conversation tracking with Lua dissectors.

The reason that "http.response_for_uri" was changed to
"http.request.full_uri" was that with the former there was no way to list
all the frames, both requests and responses. that contain a given URI. The
only way to make "http.response_for_uri" work again would be to duplicate
the request URI and the full URI and assign them different filter names.
That would greatly clutter up the Packet Detail display. Of the two filters
in question "http.request.full_uri" is far more useful and intuitive for
most users plus, as mentioned, there is a way to get the previous results.

HTTP: Request-response matching corrected

/*
*  Unlike protocols such as NFS and SMB, the HTTP protocol (RFC 9110) does not
*  provide an identifier with which to match requests and responses. Instead,
*  matching is solely based upon the order in which responses are received.
*  HTTP I/O is asynchronously ordered such that, for example, the first of four
*  GET responses is matched with the first outstanding request, the next
*  response with the second oldest outstanding request and so on (FIFO).
*  The previous method instead matched responses with the last of several
*  async requests rather than the first (LIFO), and did not handle requests
*  with no responses such as the case where one or more HTTP packets were
*  not captured. Whenever there were multiple outstanding requests, the SRT
*  (RTT) stats were incorrect, in some cases massively so.
*
*  While RFC 9110 expressly prohibits matching via byte ranges because, among
*  other things, the server may return fewer bytes than requested, the first
*  number of the range does not change. Unlike HTTP implementations, Wireshark
*  has the problem of requests/responses missing from the capture file.
*  In such cases resumption of correct matching was virtually impossible and
*  all matching was incorrect from that point on.
*

commits_data.title: HTTP: Request-response matching corrected
commits_data.message:
HTTP: Request-response matching corrected

/*
*  Unlike protocols such as NFS and SMB, the HTTP protocol (RFC 9110) does not
*  provide an identifier with which to match requests and responses. Instead,
*  matching is solely based upon the order in which responses are received.
*  HTTP I/O is asynchronously ordered such that, for example, the first of four
*  GET responses is matched with the first outstanding request, the next
*  response with the second oldest outstanding request and so on (FIFO).
*  The previous method instead matched responses with the last of several
*  async requests rather than the first (LIFO), and did not handle requests
*  with no responses such as the case where one or more HTTP packets were
*  not captured. Whenever there were multiple outstanding requests, the SRT
*  (RTT) stats were incorrect, in some cases massively so.
*
*  While RFC 9110 expressly prohibits matching via byte ranges because, among
*  other things, the server may return fewer bytes than requested, the first
*  number of the range does not change. Unlike HTTP implementations, Wireshark
*  has the problem of requests/responses missing from the capture file.
*  In such cases resumption of correct matching was virtually impossible and
*  all matching was incorrect from that point on.
*
*  The method of matching used herein is able to recover from packet loss,
*  any nummber of missing frames, and duplicate range requests. The
*  method used is explaned within the comments.
